title: Evaluate the welfare of a horse

lessons.title: Evaluating the wellbeing of a horse
lessons.html:
A structured welfare check

Welfare is about how the horse is coping, physically and mentally. Use a structured approach, such as the Five Domains: nutrition, environment, health, behavioural interactions and the resulting mental state. Evaluate both the resources given to the horse and the horse itself.

Animal-based measures

  • Body condition score (BCS): use a 1 to 9 or 0 to 5 scale. Feel the ribs, spine, withers and tail head. Too thin and obese are both welfare problems.
  • Coat and skin: shine, rain scald, lice, wounds, saddle or harness sores, rub marks.
  • Feet: overgrown, cracked or neglected hooves; lameness.
  • Eyes and nose: discharge, swelling.
  • Behaviour: alert and curious, or dull and withdrawn. Look for fear of people, aggression, and stereotypies such as crib-biting, weaving and box walking, which point to stress or boredom.
  • Vital signs: temperature, pulse and breathing when there is doubt.

Resource-based measures

  • Water: clean, available, enough for all horses.
  • Feed: enough roughage, suitable concentrates, stored safely.
  • Shelter and space: shade, protection from bad weather, safe fences, enough room.
  • Social contact: horses are herd animals; long isolation is stressful.
  • Tack and equipment: fits well, clean, in good repair.
  • Workload: suitable for age, fitness and condition, with rest days.
  • Records: vaccinations, deworming, farrier and dental care.

Record findings on a welfare assessment form with dates and photographs, so that improvement or decline can be tracked.

lessons.title: When horses need help, and how to report neglect
lessons.html:
Recognising when a horse needs assistance

Some situations need immediate action; others need a plan with the owner.

Urgent: act nowNeeds follow-up
Colic, severe lameness, suspected fractureGradual weight loss
Deep wounds, heavy bleedingOvergrown hooves
Down and unable to risePoor tack fit, mild sores
No water in hot weatherUnsuitable shelter
BCS very low (emaciated)Dental problems, quidding

For urgent cases, call the vet at once and make the horse safe. For follow-up cases, discuss with the owner or manager, agree on actions and set a date to check again. Many owners simply lack knowledge or money; education and links to welfare groups often solve the problem.

Reporting neglect and abuse

Cruelty and neglect are offences under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962. When advice does not work, or when abuse is deliberate, report it.

  1. Collect evidence: date, time, place, description of the horse (colour, markings, brand), what you saw, BCS, photos and video.
  2. Keep it factual: describe what you saw, not what you think the owner intended.
  3. Report to: the local SPCA, whose inspectors can investigate and act; or the South African Police Service, where a criminal case can be opened. Equine welfare organisations can also help.
  4. Get a reference number and keep copies of all evidence.
  5. Be prepared to give a statement and, if needed, testify.

Your own safety

Do not confront aggressive people or enter property without permission. Let the inspectors and police do their work.

Key points

  • Use a structured check covering animal-based and resource-based measures.
  • Body condition, feet, coat, behaviour and stereotypies tell you how the horse is coping.
  • Separate urgent cases (call the vet) from follow-up cases (plan with the owner).
  • Report neglect or abuse to the SPCA or police with factual evidence.
  • Stay safe; do not confront or trespass.
